sentences.text: AI Hallucination Cases is Damien Charlotin's database of legal decisions in which a court or tribunal finds or implies reliance on hallucinated material (MMRS record); its own page says it "tracks legal decisions" in cases where generative AI produced hallucinated content, "typically fake citations, but also other types of AI-generated arguments", and describes itself as "the most comprehensive database of AI hallucination cases in law".

Charlotin wrote in November 2025 that he maintains it on his personal website (FAQ), and the MMRS record gives him as its operator by his own statement; HAQQ's tracker calls him a research fellow at HEC Paris, and Wikipedia's articles on artificial intelligence and on hallucination a legal data analysis lecturer at HEC Paris and Sciences Po.

Its unit is the decision (MMRS record), which its page defines as any document "where the use of AI, whether established or merely alleged, is addressed in more than a passing reference by the court or tribunal"; it admits "only cases where the court or tribunal has explicitly found (or implied) that a party relied on hallucinated content or material", which the MMRS record states as reliance a court "explicitly finds, or implies", entering it in its self-description field and as the property that admission requires "a court finding or implication of reliance on hallucinated material".

The judgment is the courts': "I am not making that judgment, I let the courts and judges make or imply it, which is why the database is necessarily an undercount" (FAQ); HAQQ restates the bar as a court that "found, or clearly implied" reliance, accusations alone not counting, and the FAQ holds that most hallucinations are "very obvious", a made-up case name or false quote one that "cannot be a human mistake".

Its exceptions are stated twice, and the statements pull apart: its page "also covers some judicial decisions where AI use was alleged but not confirmed", "a judgment call on my part", while the FAQ says he refrains "from adding rows about cases where hallucinations are only alleged" and, in a February 2026 edit, makes an exception where the alleged hallucination comes from a judge and, absent an appeal decision or retraction, he is "bound to make a judgment call"; the MMRS record composes both as "Mere allegations are excluded, with some judgment calls admitted."

It states its boundary itself, that it "does not track the (necessarily wider) universe of all fake citations or use of AI in court filings" (its page; quoted by the MMRS record), and on the MMRS record's reading a fabricated citation enters only when a court catches and rules on it; HAQQ draws the same consequence for its reading of the count, "a fake citation nobody checks never reaches the database, so 2,202 is a floor".

Each record gives the case, the court and jurisdiction, the date, the party using AI, the AI tool, the nature of the hallucination, the outcome or sanction, the monetary penalty, details and reports (its table; the MMRS record lists the court, date, party, tool where named, nature and outcome), the nature filed as Fabricated (1,829), False Quotes (595), Misrepresented (947) or Outdated Advice (38).
Its outcomes can be filtered for monetary sanctions and disciplinary referrals, and a penalty recorded as 1 "is a placeholder, not the real figure", the amount being unknown (its page).

Its page states the record's limits: AI tools are tracked "only as disclosed or admitted by parties in court filings", with 'Unidentified' and 'Implied' as the defaults; a named tool "does not necessarily mean that tool was responsible"; offending-document dates are parsed automatically and "may occasionally be wrong", and responses when caught are extracted automatically, "indicative rather than exact".

Seeking to be exhaustive, it had identified 2,231 cases at its update of 28 October 2026 and calls itself "a work in progress" (its page; the MMRS record gives the same count as of the site's own update date), 1,514 of them from the USA, 238 from Canada, 112 from Australia and 82 from the UK, with 1,288 involving pro se litigants, 880 lawyers, 32 judges, 17 experts and 5 prosecutors (its filters; the MMRS record gives the pro se and lawyer counts).
HAQQ, reading the database's update of 19 October 2026, gives 2,202 decisions, 1,501 from the United States, 1,267 involving pro se litigants and 872 lawyers.

Charlotin started it in April 2025 while teaching Sciences Po Law School students on the "Limits and Potentials" of LLMs in law, when he looked for data on hallucinations and, finding none, decided to "tally the cases myself" (FAQ); Wikipedia dates its establishment to April 2025 and places its creation among the effects of law firms' use of generative AI for research; its period filter begins in the second quarter of 2023 (its page; MMRS record), and the MMRS record's census enters that filter as its founding.

Before 2025, the FAQ says, "we maybe had two or three cases a month", and by February 2026 the daily average was five; Wikipedia's hallucination article gives over 1,300 instances a year after its start, a LinkedIn post four months before the capture 1,600 cases, and HAQQ's series about 200 in mid-2025, 719 in January 2026 and 2,202 on 19 October 2026; its page reads "Updated daily" and was last updated on 28 October 2026, and the MMRS record gives its cadence as continuous.

The FAQ attributes the acceleration to judicial lag, the availability of LLMs and public knowledge of them, matching a profile of self-represented litigants or lawyers surprised by a tool's new AI component, and explains the share of US entries by the US legal data ecosystem, legal data in many European countries being "hoarded by legal editors".
It divides the records into pure mistakes, "the vast majority of cases", and a "(substantial) minority" involving "bad" actors (FAQ).

Cases come from referrals, scrapers and bots monitoring data sources, and keyword searches (FAQ), and readers are asked to send cases (its page); the MMRS record gives the intake as editor-curated with readers sending cases and the database growing by its editor's reading and readers' cases; the pipeline for new entries itself uses AI, "though I am careful to check it does not hallucinate" (FAQ).

It is licensed CC BY 4.0, "free to reuse, including commercially, with attribution", to be cited as "AI Hallucination Cases Database, Damien Charlotin", and its cases download as CSV (its page; MMRS record).

The FAQ gives its use as practitioners finding the cases relevant in their own jurisdiction, data analyses, and the cases as "benchmarks to fix the issue"; from it Charlotin built PelAIkan, "an automated reference checker that also detects hallucinations" (its page), and he expects no fix "at the model stage" and no reduction to zero "given the existing paradigm" (FAQ, a forecast).

"For years, we (me included) have cited without reading; but now the costs of that practice have become explicit": hallucinations, the FAQ says, "expose the epistemic hygiene the legal profession has long lacked".

The MMRS record reads it as "the census's most exact record of citation fidelity", recording attribution by the nature of the hallucination: "Each entry is a machine composition that reached a court with sources it invented or misrepresented, and the court's decision is the reception that recorded it."

It has been featured in news media "and indeed in several decisions dealing with hallucinated material", the LA Times among them in May 2025 (its page); Wikipedia cites it for counts of Canadian filings (at least 167 by 14 June 2026, with courtready.ca) and Israeli cases (at least 55 by August 2026) and, in its article on Mata v. Avianca, for that case's description as a landmark, and its article on artificial intelligence records judges' sanctions and bar warnings by 2026.
On the Overview's video cards it appears at title grain: KARE 11's "How common are AI hallucinations in court cases?" and Miller Law Group's "AI Hallucinations Got an Attorney Disbarred".

HAQQ, which discloses that it "sells a legal AI product", re-reads the live database monthly and takes off its page any number it cannot re-verify, and lists sanctions from revoked admissions to personal costs, the largest it can source about $109,700 (HAQQ); the MMRS record enters it as a candidate, "a vendor tracker built on Charlotin's count".

Matthew Lee, a barrister at Doughty Street Chambers, keeps at Natural and Artificial Law an international tracker of "Selected judicial quotations" on AI hallucination cases and fabricated or false citations, first published 16 May 2025, which "does not measure how often these issues occur", and a separate UK tracker of case records, outcomes, quotations and sources in which "inclusion is not proof of an AI hallucination or wrongdoing"; neither page names Charlotin's database, which the MMRS record's candidate list enters as "a UK companion to Charlotin's database".

The Capture Registry (2026-10-29) holds the UK tracker a separate aggregator and HAQQ's tracker, which gives the database's 2,202 decisions of 19 October (HAQQ), built on Charlotin's count, both added as candidates the census did not hold, and reads the cards as the database "already aggregated in turn: a regional companion and a vendor tracker counting its cases".

The MMRS record keeps itself apart from the entity, each assertion with a source and a basis and the lifecycle apart from the observation that saw it, records the database as active on 28 October 2026 with the roles of monitoring and reception, and relates it to the composition layer's account seated in the Capture Registry.

There (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29) the Overview at 'ai hallucination cases database' composes the database with its maker and at its size, Charlotin and 'over 2,200' being right against the 2,231 its page gives, as the field's primary record; it narrows the admission rule, which the page states as reliance the court "has explicitly found (or implied)", to 'explicitly', so that the implied cases are dropped, and lists private lawyers first where the page's filters give 1,288 pro se litigants and 880 lawyers.
